newsitem.title: USA: Key House freshman keeps distance from Contract.
newsitem.headline: Key House freshman keeps distance from Contract.

text.p: Last year, freshman Representative Jon Fox of Pennsylvania was a standard bearer for the Contract with America and House Speaker Newt Gingrich's Republican revolution.
This year, he's keeping his distance in the face of a backlash against Gingrich that has become a top issue in the re-election campaigns of Congress's Republican class of 1994.
"I've been an independent Republican," Fox told Reuters earlier this week.
"While I have agreed greatly with the speaker on a lot of the fiscal controls and trying to rein in wasteful spending, I want to make sure we have a safety net for those who are in need," Fox said.

Fox is now locked in a tough re-election battle against Democrat Joe Hoeffel, a county commissioner for Montgomery County, which encompasses the wealthy and traditionally Republican 13th Congressional district in suburban Philadelphia.
"Jon Fox has been a loyal supporter of the Gingrich revolution. Jon Fox signed the Contract with America," Hoeffel said at a campaign rally earlier this week. "The day of reckoning is coming."
Fox's stance illustrates the re-election challenges he shares with other members of Congress's class of 1994, in which 73 new Republicans were elected and won control of the House.

A blistering battle over Republican-proposed cuts in the Medicare health programme and a government shutdown over the budget diminished the popularity of Gingrich and boosted President Clinton's to the point where Democrats have a chance to recapture the House, analysts said.
"This has the potential this year of being a nationalised Congressional election ... over Newt Gingrich, Medicare, (and) shutdown of the government," said Reuters pollster John Zogby.

Political scientist Terry Madonna of Pennsylvania's Millersville University added, "What we're seeing play out in the Fox (race) is pretty much what we're seeing play out across the country, in which the Democrats are trying to position the Republican candidate as being very right-wing, very much out of the mainstream."

Nationwide polls show a nearly equal party preference in Congressional races, but these do not measure named candidates. And the preference gap has tightened after what appeared to be a Clinton-led surge for Democrats in early September.
"There is some volatility here," said Zogby.
Both Hoeffel and Fox say their internal polls show Fox leading. Hoeffel said he has closed to within striking distance at six percentage points, and Fox says he has a 17 point lead.
Fox was one of the highest-profile members of the Republican wave in 1994.
He signed the Contract with America as a candidate, and beat first-term Representative Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinsky, who cast the deciding vote in 1993 for Clinton's economic plan.
Fox returned to his district touting progress on the Contract with America after his first 100 days on the job. "They realise we've kept our word," he said of his voters then.
This year, while Democrats accuse them of being Gingrich clones, Republicans like Fox are stressing their moderate credentials and hoping to escape any anti-Gingrich backlash.
In his case, Fox said, the accusation is "artificial." He cited support for the environment, an assault weapons ban, mass transit and family planning as examples of his independence.
He also pointed to what he said were accomplishments of the last two years, including work on health care, welfare reform, regulatory reform, and attempts to balance the budget.

Democratic leaders have targeted the Fox-Hoeffel race as a top opportunity in their quest to recapture Congress. "I think we can win here," said Democratic National Committee Chairman Don Fowler, campaigning with Hoeffel last week.

But Craig Veith, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee, said the party expected a 20-30 seat gain in the Congressional elections. He said an anti-Gingrich strategy failed in a December special election in California, and would do so again.
